display_title: The Debate Over UK Bank Taxes
short_summary: A major UK union is calling for higher taxes on banks, claiming that previous policy changes resulted in billions of pounds in lost public revenue.

sources.name: The Guardian
sources.title: Tory tax break for banks has cost UK public purse £6bn, says TUC

paragraphs: A contentious debate is currently unfolding in the United Kingdom regarding the taxation of the country's most prominent financial institutions. The Trades Union Congress (TUC), an influential body representing over 5.3 million workers across England and Wales, has released a stark analysis suggesting the public purse has been deprived of £6 billion in tax revenue over the last three years. This significant shortfall is directly attributed to a 2023 policy decision by the previous Conservative administration under Chancellor Jeremy Hunt, which slashed the bank surcharge—an additional levy applied to lenders' profits—from 8% to 3%.

At the time, this reduction was intended to offset a broader increase in the standard corporation tax rate, which rose from 19% to 25%. The banking sector had lobbied heavily, arguing that higher taxes would place them at a severe competitive disadvantage compared to other global financial hubs like New York. However, the TUC contends that this tax break was remarkably ill-timed, as lenders were simultaneously reaping handsome earnings driven by rising interest rates. Indeed, the UK’s four largest lenders—HSBC, NatWest, Barclays, and Lloyds Banking Group—have collectively generated an astonishing £200 billion in pre-tax profits over the past five years.

As the government approaches the 28 October budget, the TUC is urging Chancellor John Healey to reverse these cuts to ensure banks pay their “fair share.” The union suggests that taxing these booming profits could provide essential funding to help households manage soaring energy costs, aligning with Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s broader strategy to tackle the cost of living. The TUC has proposed several scenarios: raising the surcharge to 16% could generate £24 billion over four years, while a 35% rate—matching the windfall tax imposed on energy companies—could potentially raise £60 billion.

Predictably, the banking industry remains staunchly opposed to these fiscal adjustments. David Postings, chief executive of the lobby group UK Finance, maintains that a robust banking sector is indispensable for the UK economy. He argues that profitable lenders are necessary to invest in improved customer services, issue more loans, and deliver shareholder dividends that support public savings and pensions. Furthermore, industry leaders warn that additional tax burdens would discourage investment and job creation, undermining the government's ambitions for growth.

High-profile figures have also weighed in on the matter. Jamie Dimon, the chief executive of JP Morgan, has cautioned government officials that further levies could jeopardize investment. He previously warned that he might scrap plans for a £3 billion London headquarters if the government adopted a hostile stance. As the budget deadline looms, the government faces a delicate challenge: balancing the urgent need for public revenue against the desire to maintain a thriving, competitive financial sector.

facts.fact: The TUC estimates that reducing the bank surcharge from 8% to 3% in 2023 has cost the UK government £6 billion in tax revenue.
The UK's four largest banks have generated £200 billion in pre-tax profits over the last five years.
The TUC suggests that increasing the bank surcharge to 16% could generate £24 billion in revenue over four years.
Banking industry representatives argue that higher taxes would damage the UK's competitiveness and discourage investment.
